processing: Mainly made into fully oxidised black tea; it has also been used for oolong-style tea.
harvest_season: Spring and summer flushes, as is usual for Japanese black tea.
appearance_dry: Dark twisted leaf, as is typical of Japanese black tea.
taste_profile: A seller describes a refined aroma and a strong taste; specific notes vary by maker.

brewing.notes: Western style; use freshly boiled water.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest in small lots; it is now rare, so expect limited stock and no aged versions.
description:
Hatsumomiji is a rare Japanese cultivar registered for black tea. It is worth knowing as an early step in Japanese tea breeding rather than as a mainstream name.

It is a cross between an Assam black-tea cultivar and a Japanese native tea plant, described as the first hybrid of that kind. It resists disease and wind but is not suited to cold weather.

In the cup, one seller describes a refined aroma and a strong taste. That is a shop description rather than an independent tasting note, so take it as a guide only.

Most black tea of this type in Japan now comes from later cultivars such as Benifuuki, so Hatsumomiji is a small-batch curiosity. It is also used for oolong.
history:
The cross that produced Hatsumomiji was made in 1932 at a Kagoshima prefectural test site, between an Assam cultivar and a Kagoshima native tea plant, and the cultivar was registered in 1953 for making black tea. It is described as the first hybrid between a Japanese native tea plant and an Assam black-tea cultivar.

Later black-tea cultivars bred for the same purpose, Benifuuki among them, largely took its place, and it is now seldom planted.
